# Simple Regression {.theme-section}

## Simple Regression  {.sparse-slide}

Regression and correlation are ways to identify whether two interval-ratio variables are statistically dependent 

<br>

> as the value of one variable changes, the other also tends to change

## Code Meets Question {.sparse-slide background-image="images/gears-solid-full.png" background-size="80px" background-repeat="repeat"}

::: task
{{< fa lightbulb >}} What is the relationship between literacy rate and rate of tertiary education?
:::

<br>

[**literacy rate**]{style="color: #18BC9C"}  
% of adult population that is literate

[**rate of tertiary education**]{style="color: #18BC9C"}  
the % of students enrolled/eligible within the age range

## Example df

```{r}
#| label: df
#| output-location: column

# Create columns
literacy <- c(31.7, 79.3, 85.4, 41.0, 54.7, 97.9, 92.8, 67.1, 97.8, 60.4, 87.5, 99.1)
educ <- c(3.74, 10.4, 20.4, 4.46, 9.53, 78.6, 31.5, 16.2, 65.8, 10.3, 30.8, 40.1)

# Combine into a data frame
df <- data.frame(literacy, educ)

# View the data frame
print(df)

```

## `tidy_summary()` {.sparse-slide}

`moderndive::tidy_summary()` returns commonly used summary statistics in a tidy format.  

<br>

```{r}
#| label: tidy-summary
#| output-location: fragment

df |>
  moderndive::tidy_summary()

```

##  {data-menu-title="Scatterplot"}

```{r}
#| label: scatterplot

# Create scatterplot
df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = literacy, y = educ)) +
  geom_point(color = "#18BC9C", size = 3) +
  labs(
    title = "Scatterplot of Education vs Literacy",
    x = "Literacy Rate (X)",
    y = "College enrollment (Y)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(20)
```

##  {data-menu-title="Relationships" .sparse-slide}

[**Linear relationship**]{style="color: #18BC9C"}  

When two interval-ratio level variables are related to one another we can approximate the relationship by drawing a straight line through the center of the observations on the scatterplot.  

<br>

::: {style="color: #e74c3c; font-family: 'Shadows Into Light'"}
A bivariate regression analysis finds the best possible line to summarize the observed relationship between X and Y
:::

## {data-menu-title="Scatterplot + Regression line" .sparse-slide}

```{r}
#| label: scatterplot-ols
#| code-line-numbers: "5"

# Create scatterplot with regression line
df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = literacy, y = educ)) +
    geom_point(color = "#18BC9C", size = 3) +
    geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "#3498DB") +
    labs(
      title = "Scatterplot of Education vs Literacy with Regression Line",
      x = "Literacy Rate (X)",
      y = "College enrollment (Y)"
    ) +
    theme_minimal(20)

```

## {data-menu-title="Regression equation"}

::: {style="font-size: 150%; color: #e74c3c"}
$\hat{y} = a + bX$
:::

<br>

$\hat{y}$ = the predicted score on the dependent variable

$X$ = the score on the independent variable

$a$ = the Y-intercept, or the point where the line crosses the Y-axis ($a$ is the value of $Y$ when $X$ is equal to 0).

$b$ = the slope of the regression line, or the change in $Y$ for each unit of change in $X$.

## {data-menu-title="Regression relationship"}

::: {style="font-size: 150%; color: #e74c3c"}
$\hat{y} = a + bX$
:::

<br>

[Positive relationship]{style="color: #18bc9c"}  
When $b$ is positive, then when $X$ increases, $\hat{y}$ increases

<br>

[Negative relationship]{style="color: #18bc9c"}  
When $b$ is negative, then when $X$ increases, $\hat{y}$ decreases

## {data-menu-title="Best fitting line"}

```{r, echo = FALSE}
#| label: scatterplot-lines

# Create scatterplot with regression line
df |>
  ggplot( aes(x = literacy, y = educ)) +
    geom_point(color = "#18BC9C", size = 3) +
    geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "#3498DB") +
  # Plausible but incorrect lines
    geom_abline(intercept = -20, slope = 0.9, color = "#E74C3C", linetype = "dashed", size = 1.2) +
    geom_abline(intercept = -10, slope = 0.4, color = "#F39C12", linetype = "dotted", size = 1.2) +
    geom_abline(intercept = -15, slope = 0.7, color = "#9B59B6", linetype = "twodash", size = 1.2) +
  labs(
    title = "Scatterplot of Education vs Literacy with Regression Line",
    x = "Literacy Rate (X)",
      y = "College enrollment (Y)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(20)

```

::: notes
With relationships that are imperfect, we must fit the best available line to represent the data.

ASK: Would $b$ be positive or negative? What about $a$?
:::

## {data-menu-title="Regression relationship"}

::: {style="font-size: 150%; color: #e74c3c"}
$\hat{y} = a + bX$
:::

<br>

Regression finds the best fitting line that goes through the data with the least distance (error) between all points and the line.

<br>

::: {style="color: #3498DB; font-family: 'Shadows Into Light'"}
AKA the “least squares line” referring to the least amount of squared error.
:::

::: notes
$\hat{y}$ is the predicted value of the dependent variable, based on a given value of the independent variable.
:::

## Residual = error ($e$) {.sparse-slide}

Calculated based on the difference between $Y$ and $\hat{y}$

<br>

$Y$ = observed value of $Y$ for given value of $X$  

<br>

$\hat{y}$ = predicted value of $Y$ for given value of $X$ 


## {data-menu-title="Scatterplot"}

```{r, echo=FALSE}
#| label: scatterplot-point

# Generate circle coordinates inline
theta <- seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = 100)
circle_df <- data.frame(
  x = 79.3 + 2 * cos(theta),
  y = 10.4 + 4 * sin(theta)
)

# Create scatterplot with regression line
ggplot(df, aes(x = literacy, y = educ)) +
  geom_point(color = "#18BC9C", size = 3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "#3498DB") +
# Add circle using path
  geom_path(data = circle_df, aes(x = x, y = y), color = "black", linewidth = 1.2) +
   # Add text label
  annotate("text", x = 79.3, y = 3, label = "X = 79.3, Y = 10.4", color = "black", size = 6) +
  labs(
    title = "Scatterplot of Education vs Literacy",
    x = "Literacy Rate (X)",
    y = "College enrollment (Y)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(20)

```


## {data-menu-title="Scatterplot"}

```{r, echo=FALSE}
#| label: scatterplot-predicted-point
#| message: false

# Define the new point
new_point <- data.frame(literacy = 79.3, educ = 30.67)

# Generate circle coordinates inline
theta <- seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = 100)
circle_df <- data.frame(
  x = 79.3 + 2 * cos(theta),
  y = 10.4 + 4 * sin(theta)
)

# Create scatterplot with regression line
ggplot(df, aes(x = literacy, y = educ)) +
  geom_point(color = "#18BC9C", size = 3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "#3498DB") +
# Add circle using path
  geom_path(data = circle_df, aes(x = x, y = y), color = "#18BC9C", linewidth = 1.2) +
   # Add text label
  annotate("text", x = 79.3, y = 3, label = "X = 79.3, Y = 10.4", color = "#18BC9C", size = 6) +
  # Add the new point
  geom_point(data = new_point, aes(x = literacy, y = educ), 
             color = "#E74C3C", size = 4, shape = 16) +
annotate("text", x = 79.3, y = 45,
         label = expression("X = 79.3, " * hat(y) * " = 30.67"),
         color = "#E74C3C", size = 6) +
  labs(
    title = "Scatterplot of Education vs Literacy",
    x = "Literacy Rate (X)",
    y = "College enrollment (Y)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(20)

```

## {data-menu-title="Scatterplot"}

```{r, echo=FALSE}
#| label: residual
#| message: false

# Define the new point
new_point <- data.frame(literacy = 79.3, educ = 30.67)

# Generate circle coordinates inline
theta <- seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = 100)
circle_df <- data.frame(
  x = 79.3 + 2 * cos(theta),
  y = 10.4 + 4 * sin(theta)
)

# Create scatterplot with regression line
ggplot(df, aes(x = literacy, y = educ)) +
  geom_point(color = "#18BC9C", size = 3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "#3498DB") +
# Add circle using path
geom_path(data = circle_df, aes(x = x, y = y), color = "#18BC9C", linewidth = 1.2) +
# Add text label
annotate("text", x = 79.3, y = 3, label = "X = 79.3, Y = 10.4", color = "#18BC9C", size = 6) +
# Add the new point
geom_point(data = new_point, aes(x = literacy, y = educ), 
           color = "#E74C3C", size = 4, shape = 16) +
annotate("text", x = 79.3, y = 45,
         label = expression("X = 79.3, " * hat(y) * " = 30.67"),
         color = "#E74C3C", size = 6) +
# Add a segment between the two points
annotate("segment",
         x = 79.3, y = 10.4,
         xend = 79.3, yend = 30.67,
         color = "black", linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(
    title = "Scatterplot of Education vs Literacy",
    x = "Literacy Rate (X)",
    y = "College enrollment (Y)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(20)

```


## Residual table {.sparse-slide}

```{r, echo=FALSE}
#| label: show-residuals
#| message: false

model <- lm(educ ~ literacy, data = df)

model_points <- moderndive::get_regression_points(model)

model_points |>
  select(literacy, educ, educ_hat, residual) |>
  head() |>
  kable()
```

## OLS Regression {.sparse-slide} 

::: {style="font-size: 150%; color: #e74c3c"}
$\hat{y} = a + bX$
:::

<br>

[**Least-squares line**]{style="color: #18BC9C"}  
The line where the residual sum of squares is at a minimum

<br>

[**Ordinary least-squares (OLS) regression**]{style="color: #18BC9C"}  
The statistical technique that produces the least-squares line
Sometimes referred to as linear regression

## {data-menu-title="OLS Regression" .sparse-slide}

::: {style="font-size: 150%; color: #e74c3c"}
$\hat{y} = a + bX$
:::

<br>

Calculus demonstrates the formula for $b$ and $a$ will result in a regression line that minimizes the sum of squares.  

<br>

::: task
{{< fa check-double >}} Run a regression model.
:::


## {data-menu-title="OLS Regression" .sparse-slide}

```{r}
#| label: regression
#| message: false

lm(educ ~ literacy, data = df)

```

<br>

. . . 

::: {style="font-size: 80%; color: #e74c3c"}
$\hat{y} = -33.75 + .81X$
:::

## {data-menu-title="Interpretation" .sparse-slide}

::: {style="font-size: 80%; color: #e74c3c"}
$\hat{y} = -33.75 + .81X$
:::

<br>

When the literacy rate in a country is 0, the college enrollment rate is predicted to be -33.57 ($a$) 

<br>

For every one unit increase in the literacy rate, the college enrollment rate is expected to rise by 0.81 ($b$) 

. . .

::: task
{{< fa lightbulb >}} Is this statistically significant?
:::


## `cor.test()` {.sparse-slide}

::: task
{{< fa check-double >}} Run and interpret the correlation for `educ` and `literacy`.
:::

<br>

. . .

```{r,}
#| label: cor.test
#| message: false
#| output-location: column-fragment

cor.test(
     ~ educ + literacy,
     data = df,
     method = "pearson",
     na.action = na.omit
 ) 

```


::: notes
There is a strong, positive association between the literacy rate and enrollment in tertiary education among nations.

:::


## `get_regression_table()` {.sparse-slide}

```{r}
#| label: regress-table

model <- lm(educ ~ literacy, data = df)

moderndive::get_regression_table(model)

```

<br>

::: {style="font-size: 80%"}
[**statistic**]{style="color: #18BC9C"} Test whether the coefficient is different from 0. Get the t-values by dividing the estimate by its standard error.  
  
[**p-value**]{style="color: #18BC9C"} Two-tail p-values for the test statistic  
:::

::: notes
The p value is the same for correlation and simple regression. 
:::


## Prediction {.sparse-slide}

::: {style="font-size: 100%; color: #e74c3c"}
$\hat{y} = -33.75 + .81X$
:::

<br>  

A regression equation can also be used to create predicted Y values for each value of X  

<br>

If X = 60, $Y$ is predicted to be:

$\hat{y} = -33.75 + .81(60)$  
$\hat{y} = -33.75 + 48.6$  
$\hat{y} = 15.03$  

## {data-menu-title="Prediction" .sparse-slide}

```{r, echo=FALSE}
#| label: prediction
#| message: false

# Define the new point
new_point <- data.frame(literacy = 60, educ = 15.03)

# Create scatterplot with regression line
ggplot(df, aes(x = literacy, y = educ)) +
  geom_point(color = "#18BC9C", size = 3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "#3498DB") +
# Add the new point
geom_point(data = new_point, aes(x = literacy, y = educ), 
           color = "#E74C3C", size = 4, shape = 18) +
# Add text label
annotate("text", x = 50, y = 20,
         label = expression("X = 60, " * hat(y) * " = 15.03"),
         color = "#E74C3C", size = 5) +
  labs(
    title = "Scatterplot of Education vs Literacy",
    x = "Literacy Rate (X)",
    y = "College enrollment (Y)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(20)

```

# Categorical IV {.theme-section}

## Create a categorical variable {.sparse-slide}

```{r}
#| label: cat-var
#| output-location: slide

# Use mutate and case_when to add the country_group column
df <- df |>
  mutate(
    # create the variable
    country_group = case_when(
      literacy < 50 ~ "Low Literacy",
      literacy >= 50 & literacy <= 80 ~ "Medium Literacy",
      literacy > 80 ~ "High Literacy"),
    # put the categories in a specific order
    country_group = factor(
      country_group,
      levels = c(
        "Low Literacy",
        "Medium Literacy",
        "High Literacy"))
    )


head(df)

```


##  {data-menu-title="Bar plot"}

```{r}
#| label: barplot
#| output-location: slide

df |>
  group_by(country_group) |>
  summarize(
    mean_educ = mean(educ)) |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = country_group,
      y = mean_educ,
      fill = country_group)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(
    title = "Average College Enrollment by Literacy Group",
    x = "Literacy Group",
    y = "Enrollment (%)") +
  theme_minimal(20)

```


## `get_regression_table()` {.sparse-slide}

```{r}
#| label: lm-2

model_2 <- lm(educ ~ country_group, data = df)

moderndive::get_regression_table(model_2)
```

::: notes
What does the intercept mean? Which group has the smallest proportion of college enrolles? Is it statistically significantly different (than what group?)? What proportion is enrolled in college in low literacy countries? medium literacy? 
:::

## Visualizing uncertainty

```{r} 
#| label: barplot-se
#| output-location: slide
#| code-line-numbers: "4-8, 15-20"

df |>
  group_by(country_group) |>
  summarize(
    mean_educ = mean(educ),
    se = sd(educ) / sqrt(n()),
    lower = mean_educ - 1.96 * se,
    upper = mean_educ + 1.96 * se,
    .groups = "drop") |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = country_group,
      y = mean_educ,
      fill = country_group)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(
      ymin = lower,
      ymax = upper),
    width = .15,
    linewidth = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Average College Enrollment by Literacy Group",
    x = "Literacy Group",
    y = "Enrollment (%)") +
  theme_minimal(20)
```
